title: Order
coreIdea: Train your eye to locate structure — patterns, repetition, alignment, rhythm — that already exists inside busy public space.
whyItMatters: Most street photographs fail because the frame is a collection of unrelated things. The pictures that feel inevitable succeed because the photographer first saw an underlying order and then waited for the human element to lock into it.
shootingBrief: Busy public space with continuous movement (market, transit hub, main sidewalk, ferry terminal). 45–70 minutes. Constraint: order must be the clear subject. Minimum 8 successful frames. Volume target 50–80.
One primary constraint only — do not mix exercises.
technicalFocus: Settings: Aperture priority or full manual. f/5.6–8. Shutter 1/250s minimum (prefer 1/320–1/500s). ISO under 3200 when possible.
Focusing: Zone or single-point. Pre-focus on the pattern plane (usually 3–8m). Hyperfocal at f/8 mid-zoom is useful.
Stance: Walk slowly. Small lateral shifts change alignments more than zooming. Camera ready at chest or eye level.
Light: Side or hard directional light reveals structure. Flat overcast flattens patterns.
failureModes: Forcing patterns that are not really there.
Too many competing elements so order disappears.
Shooting before the alignment is clean.

goodVsExcellent.good: You can point to the pattern and the viewer can see it.
goodVsExcellent.excellent: The order feels discovered rather than imposed. Removing any single element weakens the picture.

title: Events
coreIdea: Photograph the temporary organization of attention — the moment a group of people share a single focus.
whyItMatters: Ordinary street is diffuse. An event creates hierarchy: a clear center and a ring of reaction. Learning to work both the center and the edges builds anticipation, spatial control, and the ability to read collective body language.
shootingBrief: Any small public event or moment of shared attention. 45–70 minutes. Capture both the focus and the reaction. Minimum 6 clear event frames. Volume 40–70.
technicalFocus: Settings: AF-C, f/4–5.6, shutter 1/320s or faster.
Focusing: Continuous on the central subject or strongest reacting face.
Stance: Start on the perimeter. Move in only when geometry supports it.
Distance: 2–6 meters. Wider for context; longer to isolate reaction.
failureModes: Only photographing the center and missing the reaction.
Getting so close you become part of the event.

goodVsExcellent.good: You show that something is happening and people are reacting.
goodVsExcellent.excellent: The reaction carries equal or greater weight than the event. Spatial layers are clear.

title: Sequences
coreIdea: Work one situation across multiple intentional frames so the best picture emerges from sustained attention rather than a single lucky press.
whyItMatters: Single-frame hunting produces average results. Sequences force you to stay, adjust position, and recognize the exact moment the elements lock.
shootingBrief: Choose 3–4 situations. For each, make a deliberate sequence of 6–12 frames. Later select the strongest single frame from each. Volume 50–80. No spray-and-pray.
technicalFocus: Settings: Lock exposure across the sequence unless light changes. Prefer single frame.
Focusing: Pre-focus or continuous on the key plane. Keep focus plane consistent.
Stance: Small adjustments between frames. Do not reframe wildly.
failureModes: Changing composition so frames no longer relate.

goodVsExcellent.good: One frame from the set is clearly stronger.
goodVsExcellent.excellent: The chosen frame is stronger because of what the other frames taught you about timing and position.

title: Lining Up
coreIdea: Align separate elements in the frame so they form one deliberate graphic or narrative relationship.
whyItMatters: This is the skill that turns a picture containing interesting things into a constructed picture. Precise alignment makes frames feel inevitable rather than lucky.
shootingBrief: Wait for or create clean alignments. Minimum 6 frames where alignment is obvious and intentional. Both orientations. Volume 40–70.
technicalFocus: Focusing: On the plane where the critical alignment happens.
Stance: Micro-movements of body and camera matter more than zoom.
failureModes: Including distractions that break the alignment.
Moving too much instead of waiting.

goodVsExcellent.excellent: The alignment is exact, the rest of the frame supports it, and the picture collapses if any key element is removed.

title: Waiting
coreIdea: Choose a strong background or stage and commit to it until the right element enters.
whyItMatters: Hunting produces quantity. Waiting produces pictures that feel inevitable because the stage was already resolved before the subject arrived.
shootingBrief: Select 2–3 strong backgrounds. Commit 10–15 minutes to each. Photograph only when something worth including enters. Minimum 5 frames. Volume 30–50.
technicalFocus: Settings: Pre-set exposure for the background. Zone or single-point pre-focused on subject plane.
Focusing: Fixed zone or hyperfocal preferred.
Stance: Camera at ready height. Minimal movement once positioned.
failureModes: Leaving after four or five minutes.

goodVsExcellent.excellent: Subject and background complete each other so precisely the picture looks pre-arranged.
